tier_reason: The README table has first-party Google Benchmark numbers against std::string_view. Benchmark code is public (benchmarks/api/string_view_find.cpp, string_view_search_scenarios.cpp), but the README gives no CPU model (only '12x 2096 MHz'), no compiler, no flags, and no stdlib, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: find_first_of: zuu 6.11 ns vs std::string_view 15.7 ns (~2.5x); find (substring): 11.1 vs 14.1 ns (~1.3x); rfind (substring): 11.4 vs 16.7 ns (~1.4x); find (char): 1.56 vs 2.24 ns (~1.4x); find_last_of: 11.0 vs 14.7 ns (~1.3x); rfind (char): 2.39 vs 2.50 ns (tie). zuu is SLOWER on find_first_not_of (6.22 vs 5.01 ns, ~20% slower) and find_last_not_of (6.82 vs 5.00 ns, ~26% slower). (ns values and approximate ratios are verbatim from the README table.)
corrections.caveats: No LICENSE file and no license field in vcpkg.json (usability 'reference'); 0 stars, very early-stage project. The README does not state the compiler, flags, or stdlib for the benchmark run (CMakePresets.json defaults to clang++ with C++23, but the run is not tied to a preset). Hardware is given only as '12x 2096 MHz CPU'. Every benchmark uses one short (~95-char) haystack. zuu is 20-26% slower than std::string_view on find_first_not_of and find_last_not_of.

notes: The README numbers match the record exactly. I added the find_last_of win and the two not_of losses that the record left out. Which stdlib was the baseline (libstdc++, libc++, or MSVC STL) is unknown, so baseline_stdlib stays [].

tier_reason: The blog compares against libstdc++ std::string and folly::fbstring only in SVG bar charts. The charts have ns axes but no stated values, and the text has no numbers. Compiler, flags, and hardware are all unstated. The harness is public in a gist. The project is notable (3,333 stars), so the record is kept at D.

corrections.workload: nanobench microbenchmarks with a small ('foo') and a large (128-char) string: construction, copy-construction, find, and substr. They compare jank's persistent_string with libstdc++ std::string and folly::fbstring. The gist also has equality-comparison benchmarks, but the blog does not chart them.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Blog text, per chart: 'jank constructs small strings the fastest and ties with std::string for large strings'; 'ties with folly for copying small strings and seriously beats both when copying large strings'; 'ties with std::string for large and small string searches'; 'ties with folly for small substrings and seriously beats both when creating large substrings'. Overall it 'either ties or outperforms the fastest in every benchmark'. The page states no numeric values; results appear only as SVG bar charts.
corrections.caveats: The page states no exact numbers (bar charts only). Compiler, flags, and CPU are not stated. libc++ is mentioned but not benchmarked. In the gist, the std::string baseline is std::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, native_allocator<char>> (jank's GC allocator), not std::allocator. persistent_string lives inside the jank compiler, not in a standalone library. The record is kept at Tier D only because the project is notable (3.3k stars).

notes: The qualitative claim is verified verbatim. The SVG files contain only axis ticks and legends, no bar value labels. Approximate values could be read from the bar geometry, but I did not use them. Metadata checks out: MPL-2.0, 3,333 stars, last commit 2026-09-21.

tier_reason: PLDI '22 paper, Sec. 5.2 and Fig. 12. It states GCC 9.2.1 -O3, 4x Intel Xeon E7-8867 v4, jemalloc, and numactl -i all. The benchmark code is public in the repo (benchmarks/bench_queue.cpp, which has the weak_ptr_queue, jss_queue, and CRDoubleLinkQueue variants). The tier stays A; the verdict is downgrade only because the claim was overstated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: CDRC atomic weak pointers vs just::thread: 4.2x faster at P=8 and 10x faster at P=192 (paper Sec. 5.2). At P=1 (off-plot), the paper says the hand-tuned 'original' manual-reclamation queue is 4.5x faster than CDRC and 67x faster than just::thread, which puts CDRC ~15x ahead of just::thread at P=1 (derived from page data: 67/4.5). Versus the manual original, CDRC is 4.5x slower at P=1, 19% slower at P=8, and 33% slower at P=192.
corrections.caveats: The paper's 67x figure at P=1 is the manual 'original' implementation vs just::thread, not CDRC vs just::thread; CDRC's own P=1 margin is ~15x (derived). The baseline is just::thread, a commercial library of atomic shared and weak pointers, not libstdc++/libc++/MSVC STL atomic<weak_ptr>. The paper's separate 2x-3x throughput claim is against earlier concurrent reference-counting implementations, not std::shared_ptr. The last commit on the default branch is 2022-07-03 (the repo shows a push on 2024-02-18).

notes: Downgrade because the record credited CDRC with the paper's 67x figure, which belongs to the manual baseline. Its claim that CDRC is 19-33% slower 'over the same range' was also wrong at P=1 (4.5x slower there). Tier A still holds: PLDI '22 paper, full setup stated, benchmark code in the repo. Metadata checks out: MIT, 174 stars, not archived.

tier_reason: The README 'Speed benchmarks' section compares oup with std::weak_ptr/shared_ptr using public code (tests/speed_benchmark.cpp). Each run names the compiler and CPU: gcc 9.4.0 on a Ryzen 5 2600, MSVC 16.11.3 on an i7-7800X, and Emscripten on a Ryzen 5 2600. Flags are stated only as 'all optimizations turned on (except LTO)', so Tier A is borderline.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Dereference observer, relative to raw T* = 1 (median across object types). gcc 9.4.0/libstdc++-9/Ryzen 5 2600: weak/shared 3.5 vs observer 1.0 (obs_unique and obs_sealed), ~3.5x. MSVC 16.11.3/MS-STL/i7-7800X: 9.4 vs 1.4 (obs_unique) and 0.8 (obs_sealed), ~6.7x-11.8x. Emscripten 2.0.34/libc++/Node.js 14.15.5/Ryzen 5 2600: 38.7 vs 1.0, ~38.7x. Create observer: 1.6 vs 1.6 (gcc), 5.3 vs 1.6 (MSVC), 14.8 vs 2.3 (Emscripten). (Ratios derived from page data.)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.4.0 (libstdc++-9), MSVC 16.11.3 (MS-STL), Emscripten 2.0.34 (libc++); 'all optimizations turned on (except LTO)', exact flags not listed
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 2600, Linux 5.15.0 (gcc run); Intel i7-7800X, Windows 10.0.19043 (MSVC run); AMD Ryzen 5 2600, Node.js 14.15.5 + Linux 5.1.0 (Emscripten/libc++ run)
corrections.caveats: oup is unique-ownership only and not thread-safe; std::weak_ptr::lock() does atomic refcount work, so part of the dereference advantage comes from dropping thread safety. Creating the owner pointer is slower than std::unique_ptr. The README says the benchmarks were last run for oup v0.7.1, so they may not reflect current code. The Emscripten/libc++ run is WebAssembly on Node.js, not native.

notes: The record's numbers (1.0 vs 3.5 on gcc) match the README. I marked the ~3.5x ratio as derived and added the MSVC and Emscripten/libc++ rows, which show larger gaps. Metadata checks out: MIT, 42 stars, last commit 2026-09-05.

tier_reason: The CxxFunctionBenchmark suite (various.cpp) is public, but its README 'Sample Result' says only MSVC 15.9.4 Release, with no CPU model. The Delegate author (bdiamand) generated these numbers in PRs #23 and #25, which added Delegate and rewrote the sample-result block, so they are first-party numbers in a modest (98-star) suite: Tier C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Delegate beats std::function in all 7 invocation categories of the CxxFunctionBenchmark various.cpp sample result (MSVC 15.9.4): function_pointer 0.2101s vs 0.2640s (~1.26x); compile_time_function_pointer 0.1324 vs 0.1884 (~1.42x); compile_time_delegate 0.1395 vs 0.1906 (~1.37x); heavy_functor 0.1586 vs 0.1897 (~1.20x); non_assignable 0.1402 vs 0.1860 (~1.33x); lambda_capture 0.1585 vs 0.1757 (~1.11x); stateless_lambda 0.1325 vs 0.1799 (~1.36x). Ratios are derived from page data. Delegate is the fastest of the 13 implementations in 5 of 7 categories; in heavy_functor and lambda_capture others are equal or slightly faster (stdex::function 0.1579, func::function 0.1578).
corrections.workload: Invocation timing in CxxFunctionBenchmark various.cpp, int(int) signature, across seven call patterns: function_pointer, compile_time_function_pointer, compile_time_delegate, heavy_functor, non_assignable, lambda_capture, and stateless_lambda.
corrections.license: Custom permissive notice in the delegate.h header (not an OSI-approved license; no LICENSE file)
corrections.caveats: The Delegate author (bdiamand) produced the sample-result numbers via PRs to jamboree/CxxFunctionBenchmark in Jan 2019. The run is independent-suite code, not independently run. CPU model not stated. Tested only against MSVC STL std::function. Delegate is not the fastest in every category. The license is a custom permissive header notice, not OSI-approved, so usability is 'reference'. Delegate's own repo has no benchmark.

notes: Downgrade for two reasons. First, 'consistently fastest of 13' is false for heavy_functor and lambda_capture (the vs-std::function wins do hold in all 7 categories). Second, the numbers came from the Delegate author's own PRs, so the tier drops B to C. Metadata checks out: 43 stars, last commit 2022-07-27 (abandoned), not a fork.
